opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it usually starts with whether there's something I personally wish existed. A lot of what I've worked on came from noticing a task I kept doing over and over that felt like it should be automated: digging through dozens of sources, synthesizing information, writing it up. When a problem annoys me personally, I'm much more motivated, and I usually have good intuition for what a good outcome looks like.

The second thing is whether the timing is right. I like problems at the edge of what the models can almost do: not trivially solved, but close enough that with the right training data, the right environment, and a lot of iteration, you can get something genuinely useful. If it's too far out, you spend all your time fighting the model. If it's too easy, it's probably not that differentiated.

And the last piece is real-world value. I get excited about things where, if they work, people save hours or days of work, or can do things they couldn't do before. Being able to point at a concrete use case, like someone doing a literature review, a market analysis, or a big purchase decision, and say "this would make their life meaningfully better," keeps me grounded. Otherwise it's easy to get lost optimizing benchmarks that don't translate into anything people care about.

r001.rationale: She says product ideas often start with something she personally wishes existed, and describes motivation from personally annoying tasks she wants automated.

fable-5.1.text:
I think for me it really comes down to two things. The first is whether I actually want to use it myself. With Deep Research, for example, I was already spending hours doing this kind of work, going through papers, pulling together information from a bunch of different sources, and I just wanted something that could do that for me. When you're building something you personally want, you have really good taste about what's working and what isn't, because you're the user.

The second thing is whether the capability is close to being possible but not quite there yet. The most exciting place to be is right at the frontier, where the model can almost do the thing. That means you have to actually do the hard work on the research and product side to get it over the line, and it's not obvious how to do it. If it's something the models can already do easily, lots of people will build it. If it's way too far out, you end up spinning your wheels. So I look for that sweet spot where it's genuinely hard, I care about the outcome, and I think if we get it to work it would be meaningfully useful to a lot of people.

And honestly, a lot of it is also just who you get to work with. I've been really lucky to work with people where we could iterate incredibly fast between the research and the product, and that's what makes it fun.

r001.rationale: She says a key factor is whether she wants to use the product herself, using Deep Research as an example of something she personally wanted.

astra-6.text: I’m drawn to products that solve a problem I’ve experienced myself. That gives me a much stronger intuition for what would actually be useful, and it makes me want to keep working on the details until they’re right. I also like working on things where there’s room to experiment—where you can put something in people’s hands, learn from how they use it, and discover that the most valuable version is a little different from what you initially imagined.

r001.rationale: The response says she is drawn to products that solve a problem she has experienced, but does not clearly say anticipated personal use motivates her choice.

sol-6.1.text: I’m usually drawn to products that solve a problem I’ve felt myself. I want to understand why someone would use it, what’s frustrating about the way they do things today, and how we could make that better. I also like working on things where there’s a lot to figure out—where you can build something, put it in people’s hands, and learn from how they actually use it.

r001.rationale: She says she is drawn to products solving a problem she has felt herself, but does not say that she expects or intends to use the product personally.
